stories.topic: A field born from a satellite's side effect
stories.summary: US government satellites were photographing the Earth at night for unrelated purposes. Analysts noticed that the images were picking up the light over cities, and that a city's light footprint grew as the city prospered. That led to a conjecture: could light seen from space be used to infer economic activity? The early data was crude. Pixels were 3 km by 3 km, bright cities saturated and got top-coded, and readings came once a year. Then in 2011 NASA and NOAA launched the VIIRS sensor package, which photographs the world every night at 1:30 AM with pixels of roughly 700–800 metres.
stories.insight: Whole research fields can grow out of accidental by-products of someone else's project. The data was always there; someone just had to look at it with a different question.
stories.quote: clever analysts started seeing that by mistake you were picking up the light over cities

stories.topic: The poster on the wall that Ajay refused to use
stories.summary: At NIPFP, his colleagues Shekhar Hari Kumar and Shubho Roy were passionate about nighttime lights. They made beautiful maps and put up a poster in the office. Ajay held back for years. His CMIE training told him never to use a measure casually. Only when Ayush Patnaik started working intensely inside the VIIRS data did he dive in. He notes that the World Bank publishes a district-level dataset for India, and that many economists simply download it and hope nothing is wrong.
stories.insight: Rigour sometimes means not using exciting data until you truly understand its innards. Being early matters less than being right.
stories.quote: Either I will have extreme mastery on understanding the innards and the difficulties and the limitations and the trustworthiness of a measure, or I will not use it at all.

stories.topic: Why Bombay seemed to go dark every July
stories.summary: To sanity-check the data, the team looked at places they knew, such as Bandra West versus Bandra East. They found that Bombay's radiance collapsed every July, which made no economic sense. NASA/NOAA classify each night as cloudy or cloud-free, discard the cloudy nights, and average the rest. In July only about three of 31 nights pass. The team reasoned that those 'cloud-free' nights in the monsoon still carry wisps of cloud that dim the signal. By contrast, January yields about 25 good nights out of 31. So the fraction of cloud-free days could serve as a proxy for bias. They built a deliberately conservative correction and checked it on other cities. Dubai, cloud-free all year, barely changed. Monsoon cities like Johannesburg did. The paper and a Julia package are public.
stories.insight: Local ground truth can expose a bias that even great institutions miss. Knowing that Bombay is never really clear in July was the clue that cracked the problem.
stories.quote: We know that there are no cloud free days in July in Bombay.

stories.topic: Swedish intelligence beat the academics to it
stories.summary: When the Russia-Ukraine war began, Ajay, Susan Thomas and Ayush Patnaik thought of studying Russia with nighttime lights. They held off because 'there are like 500 labs in the world' that could do it, and surely the Europeans would. They went back to studying households in Karnataka. Years passed and no good paper on the Russian economy appeared, while the idea kept 'waking up every three days'. Then in 2024 Swedish intelligence publicly said nighttime lights over Russia had fallen sharply in 2023. Amit remarked that the intelligence agencies have skin in the game. Ajay's under-resourced team decided to do the work themselves.
stories.insight: Don't assume an obvious piece of research is already being done. People who need an answer to act can outrun people who only need it to publish. If you want something done, do it yourself.
stories.quote: Intelligence agencies in advanced economies are using nighttime lights data and the damn academics are not.

stories.topic: Russia breaks every method built for India
stories.summary: Studying Russia threw up surprises. The country was too big to load into a computer's memory, so it had to be cut into provinces, and the largest province is still bigger than India. In summer the sun is shining at 1:30 AM in St Petersburg, so the 'night' photo isn't night. Faint moonlight reflecting off the empty vastness of Siberia added up to fake radiance. Their background-noise algorithms had been tuned for the much smaller deserts of Rajasthan. The Aurora Borealis produced a huge amount of light over Ukraine in 2019. Gas flares also had to be filtered out.
stories.insight: Methods that work under one set of conditions can fail badly in another. You only catch these traps by staying close to your data.
stories.quote: you'll be pleased to know that in the summer at one thirty AM in Saint Petersburg, the sun is shining.

stories.topic: How WWII was decided by factories, not battles
stories.summary: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and 'poked the giant', Hitler foolishly declared war on America the very next day. He thought he was obliged to, and did not understand America. Once American production mobilised, it was game over. Japan, an island, depended on raw materials shipped from across East Asia. The US Navy strangled those supply chains. Occupied Europe could not match the US, Britain with its empire, and the Soviet Union combined. Allied bombers flew from Britain to destroy German factories one by one. Germany never built a long-range bomber, so Soviet factories moved deep inland stayed safe.
stories.insight: Long wars are won by production capacity and by understanding your adversary. Battlefield brilliance can't overcome a hopeless economic balance.
stories.quote: And when American production was mobilized on one side, it was really game over.

recommendations.item: Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War
recommendations.creator: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: The xKDR paper at the heart of the episode, which Amit brings up as the work shedding light on 'the greatest question of our age'.
recommendations.reason: It uses carefully corrected nighttime lights to read Russia's economy while official data is withheld. It finds the economy roughly flat from January 2019 to January 2025, damage along the Ukraine and European borders, and a 245 km eastward shift in the economy's centre of mass.

recommendations.item: But Clouds Got In My Way: Bias and bias correction of VIIRS nighttime lights data in the presence of clouds
recommendations.creator: Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Anshul Tayal & Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: The methods paper behind the Bombay-in-July discovery.
recommendations.reason: It documents a cloud-related bias in NASA/NOAA data and offers a conservative correction. Ajay argues there is no case for anyone to keep using the uncorrected data.

recommendations.item: NighttimeLights.jl (xKDR's nighttime lights data and code on GitHub)
recommendations.creator: xKDR Forum
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions the public Julia package; Amit points readers to the GitHub link in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Anyone can apply the bias corrections, change parameters and experiment with the data themselves. Amit calls this the 'spirit of inquiry'.

recommendations.item: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
recommendations.creator: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
recommendations.context: Invoked while showing the North Korea vs South Korea night-time image.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it 'answer one' to the question of whether socialism works. The satellite image of the Korean peninsula is answer two.

recommendations.creator: Joni Mitchell
recommendations.context: Prompted by the title of Ajay's methods paper, 'But Clouds Got In My Way'.
recommendations.reason: Amit asks Joni Mitchell fans to appreciate the allusion and listen to 'the great song' linked in the show notes.

recommendations.item: The Future of War (Episode 112 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay links the Russia analysis back to this recent episode.
recommendations.reason: It sets out how modern war has changed, including long-range standoff weapons. That framing explains why Russian regions far from the Ukrainian border are being damaged.

recommendations.item: What Should India Do? (Episode 114 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced while explaining Hitler's failure to understand America.
recommendations.reason: That episode argued that dealing with America and China requires deep knowledge of them. Hitler is the cautionary tale of what happens without it.

recommendations.item: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit recalls it at the end, after hearing about nighttime lights as unconventional data.
recommendations.reason: In that episode Amit and his guests (Niti Gupta, Hamsini Hariharan and Devika) invented non-traditional measures of women's empowerment on the fly. It is the seed of the next episode's theme.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: An old column of Amit's, cited as his contribution to Metrics of Empowerment.
recommendations.reason: It argues that rising divorce rates can signal women being empowered to leave bad marriages, a neat example of a creative proxy metric.

core_ideas.concept: Nighttime lights as a measure of prosperity
core_ideas.explanation: Every night at 1:30 AM, satellites record how much light comes out of each roughly 700–800 m patch of Earth. Streetlights, compound walls, cars, all-night petrol pumps and restaurants rise with prosperity, so brightness tracks economic activity. Bandra West shows up brighter than Bandra East. Ships even reveal congestion at ports.
core_ideas.quote: Look at the world at night. And if there is a successful human society down there, it will have lit up the place with light.

core_ideas.explanation: Light rises with income but not in a straight line, and the data has traps. Taller buildings trap light under their roofs. LEDs register about 34% less light at the sensor, so the shift to LEDs understates growth. Faint moonlight summed over a vast area can make Jaisalmer look as bright as Bandra West, whose GDP is ten times bigger. And at rich-country levels, more income doesn't mean more lights, so Switzerland and the US look alike. Ajay thinks economists got over-excited treating it as a straight replacement for GDP data.
core_ideas.quote: Nighttime lights is far away from GDP. It's a proxy for economic activity.

core_ideas.concept: A statistical system with a twist
core_ideas.explanation: NASA, NOAA, the European Space Agency and the Japanese space agency release maintained, regularly updated satellite data free to the world. This is measurement without the institutional complexity of a statistics office walking the country. Because each pixel is small, you can draw any boundary, such as the 300 urban local bodies of Karnataka. You get city-level, monthly signals, whereas GDP comes out once a year with a long lag.
core_ideas.quote: These are public goods being produced using government money. So it is a statistical system with a twist.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay holds that half the battle in economics is measuring something correctly. Analysis and theorising come after. Without depth in measurement you get garbage in, garbage out, and waste everyone's time. His advice to economists is to love their data deeply.
core_ideas.quote: I think that's the core intellectual honesty of being a good economist, which is you must be passionate about measurement. You have to really wage war on measurement.

core_ideas.concept: Sanity-check data against what you know
core_ideas.explanation: Before trusting a new dataset, test it on places you understand. Is Bandra West brighter than Bandra East, and Bandra East brighter than Karjat? Local knowledge, like knowing Bombay is never clear in July, is what exposes hidden biases.
core_ideas.quote: these basic facts should be there in the data, otherwise, there is some golmaal, something is amiss.

core_ideas.explanation: When fixing a bias you can be aggressive and risk new errors, or conservative and certain. Ajay's team chose to correct only where they were absolutely sure. The aim was a fix so safe that everyone should adopt it, leaving bolder corrections to later researchers.
core_ideas.quote: So we undercorrect, but we are absolutely sure that we are adding value by our undercorrection.

core_ideas.explanation: A long war of attrition is decided by whether the economy can supply guns, butter and soldiers. Ukraine doesn't need to produce much itself, because it is backed by Europe: guns are made in Germany and butter in the UK. Russia is an Italy-sized economy whose only important patron is North Korea.
core_ideas.quote: First, we've always known that strategic war is a war of economics.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay lists four. One to two million of the most educated and richest people fled. Western sanctions made buying, paying and earning hard. The economy was rejigged toward war production at the expense of civilian output. And Ukrainian standoff weapons are now hitting its industry.
core_ideas.quote: So you have more guns, you have less butter.

core_ideas.explanation: In WWII, Soviet factories were safe deep inland because Germany had no long-range bomber. Ukraine's deep-strike weapons now reach hundreds to 2,000 km into Russia, destroying factories and refineries, and these weapons arrived only in the last six to nine months. Ajay draws an implication: if China invades Taiwan, expect hundreds of kilometres of the Chinese coast to face the same treatment.
core_ideas.quote: So imagine there's a war going on at Delhi. But there are deep strike weapons coming and hitting near the Karnataka Tamil Nadu border.

core_ideas.concept: Reading a wartime economy from space
core_ideas.explanation:
Russia has, 'as they should', withheld economic data because it is now strategic, so satellites fill the gap. Ajay compares January to January, since Russian Januaries are dark at 1:30 AM and cloud-free. The findings:
- Overall radiance in 2025 is about where it was in 2019: war production up, civilian economy down.
- Regions near Ukraine are hit by strikes.
- Regions near the Baltic states and Europe are hurt by sanctions reversing the gains from trade.
- Eastern borders, where sanctions aren't enforced, are fine.
- The economy's centre of mass has moved east.
For January 2026, Ajay is watching two opposing forces: Trump easing sanctions and Ukraine improving its deep-strike weapons.
core_ideas.quote: the center of mass has moved east by 245 kilometers. So the Russian economy is shifting in its character away from the west to the east.

core_ideas.explanation: Beyond GDP-style proxies, creative indicators can reveal how a society actually lives. Examples include rising divorce rates as a sign of women's empowerment, or who orders more from grocery apps. Amit proposes devoting the next episode to such metrics.
core_ideas.quote: there are actually many, many unconventional kinds of metrics that we can use to get insights on society.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens with an acrostic poem, 'Nighttime Lights', whose first letters spell 'I LOVE FREEDOM'. He explains the phrase made 'the poet in me arose. I was about to say was aroused, but that's not the right word.' After reading it to a dry-eyed Ajay he adds: 'I can see that you aren't tearing up. This is very sad. Maybe we should make AI make you cry.'
Ajay on the North Korea vs South Korea night image as the answer to whether socialism works: 'you should have tried it on hamsters first.'

Ajay explaining why light stops tracking income at the top: 'We have Amit Varma... when your income doubles, is your lighting going to double? No. You're done. You've reached the zenith of human prosperity where there is no possibility of your buying any more lights.' Amit: 'Also double of zero is zero, but continue.'
The word 'incandescent' sparks a quatrain from Amit: 'I told her she was incandescent when I met her for a lark. She looked at me with twinkling eyes and said I was too dark.'

Ajay's passion for measurement inspires another: 'I said to her, I'll treasure you, I love you bit by bit. But first, my love, I'll measure you to make sure that I fit.' When Ajay says he's getting better and better, Amit replies: 'You weren't a good economist at twenty or thirty or forty, it took some time.'
Amit: 'the reason you're my favorite economist friend... Sorry to other economist friends who might be watching this, oh wait, I have none.'

Ajay on NASA and NOAA giving away data: 'we shouldn't say this too loudly because... if Donald Trump is an enthusiastic watcher of Everything is Everything, he will complain that these are global public goods and the US government is not being compensated.'
After Ajay says Hitler didn't understand America, Amit: 'I don't think anybody understands America. I don't think America understands America.'
Ajay on why January is the month to study Russia, with short days and no clouds: 'January is the time to peek into the Kremlin and look at what Putin [is] doing on his morning walk.'

Ajay describes Russia as a 'petroleum producing country which also happens to have nuclear weapons'. On why it flares so much gas: 'Russia is a Communist country, they don't know how to handle the gas.'

Amit wonders how 'many a slip between cup and lip' ever originated: 'There's a cup, there's a lip. Generally there are no slips.' He then spins it into a cricket riff about Vivian Richards, playing India, about to raise his cup to his lip.
Amit had asked about 'the light' Ajay's paper sheds on the war. When Ajay reveals it is titled 'Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War', the response is: 'lame minds think alike.'
Ajay's advice to every economist, in romantic mode: 'please love your data deeply and you know, look deep in her eyes because without that you'll never make progress.'
Freddy, the show's 'best friend', named after 'Freddie' Bastiat, in turn named after 'Freddy' Hayek.
The methods paper's title, 'But Clouds Got In My Way', nods to Joni Mitchell's 'Both Sides Now', which Amit asks fans to appreciate.
The iconic satellite image of North and South Korea at night, shown for 2012 and 2025, which Ajay calls 'one of the most influential pictures in the history of the socialism question.'

Pearl Harbor, where Japan 'poked the giant', followed by Hitler declaring war on America the next day. Ajay notes Hitler had no idea that 'a MAGA isolationist problem was alive and well in America at that time.'
